newsitem.title: CANADA: Loewen rebuffs sweetened Service bid.
newsitem.headline: Loewen rebuffs sweetened Service bid.

text.p: The Loewen Group Inc. said Thursday its board unanimously rejected Service Corp. International's sweetened $2.9 billion hostile takeover bid and urged stockholders not to tender their shares.

Service, North America's biggest operator of funeral homes and cemeteries, last week offered $45 a share in stock for Loewen, its closest competitor. Loewen previously rejected a $43 a share offer from Service and had been widely expected to rebuff the higher bid.

Going on the attack, Loewen filed an anti-trust lawsuit against Houston-based Service and said scrutiny of the deal by regulators had broadened to include more U.S. states as well as the U.S. and Canadian governments.

Loewen said its board concluded "the best way to maximize value for shareholders is through continued implementation of the company's long-term business plan as an independent company. The board believes the company will continue to build shareholder value through growth, especially growth through acquisitions, and through enhanced profitability."

Loewen's investment bankers, Smith Barney and Nesbitt Burns, gave the company opinions that the offer was inadequate, Loewen said. Loewen's board also adopted a "golden parachute" severance plan for key executives that would be triggered by a change in control.
Loewen underscored what it said were "significant" conditions attached to the bid including the tendering of 75 percent of Loewen's outstanding common and preferred shares.
Reaching that threshold is expected to be difficult because Loewen Chief Executive Ray Loewen holds about 15 percent of the company's shares and insiders hold another 5 percent.
Service's bid has not yet gone into effect while the Securities and Exchange Commission reviews filings associated with the deal, so no date for a tender offer has been set.
Investment analysts doubted Service would be deterred by Loewen's announcement. But they viewed it as unlikely Service would increase its offer again right away.
"This is no surprise. Nobody expected this to be accepted by Loewen, so the game continues," said Dean Witter analyst Todd Richter.

Service had no immediate response to Loewen's announcement. It previously said it would consider raising its offer if Loewen would agree to negotiate a transaction, which appeared out of the question in light of Loewen's response Thursday.

Before the news, Loewen's stock closed unchanged at $38.875 in New York, while Service shares dipped 25 cents to $29.375. After soaring on news of Service's first offer on Sept. 17, Loewen's stock has fallen sharply over the past week as traders anticipated a protracted battle.

Loewen said the "anti-competitive effects" of the deal raised regulatory scrutiny in several states, including New York, Florida, Hawaii, Texas, California and Tennessee and from the Federal Trade Commission. It said the Canadian Competition Bureau was also investigating the deal.
This represents a broadening of regulatory scrutiny into the deal. Loewen previously said only that Florida and the Federal Trade Commission were looking into the offer.
"As a result of the significant anti-trust issues ... there is significant uncertainty as to whether the conditions of the Service proposal will be met," it said.

Loewen reiterated its claims that Service was seeking to buy it "on the cheap" and eliminate competition. The two companies have often confronted each other as they sought to buy up independent funeral homes and cemeteries.
Loewen's anti-trust case was filed against Service and its 40-percent owned affiliate Equity Corp. International in U.S. District Court in New York.

The lawsuit alleges the deal would "substantially lessen competition in the markets for locally offered funeral and cemetery services, 'pre-need' funeral services, and the funeral home and cemetery acquisition markets."
It claims Service and Equity are conspiring to eliminate Loewen as a competitor.
